newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - HK's Patten and Tung like chalk and cheese.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - HK's Patten and Tung like chalk and cheese.

text.p: With just 100 days to go to Hong Kong's handover to China, its future leader is racing against the clock as he struggles to evolve from successful but low-key businessman to political leader.

Groomed from boyhood to take over his father's vast shipping empire, Tung Chee-hwa was plucked by Beijing from relative obscurity late last year at the age of 59 and handed an awesome task. Run post-colonial Hong Kong for us, he was told.
Hong Kong was promised considerable autonomy. Capitalism will be preserved for 50 years but the territory must not become a base for subversion likely to infect China.

Tung has a difficult act to follow. Chris Patten. who spent more than two decades in the hurly burly of British parliamentary politics before he arrived on July 9, 1992, to become the 28th and last colonial governor of Hong Kong.
"They are like chalk and cheese," said a senior government official who has worked alongside both men
Both are family men. Both enjoy rock-solid marriages. Both are worldly and enjoy sports, their friends and colleagues say.
But Patten is a liberal while Tung is deeply conservative.
NOT PLAIN SAILING

The past few months have not been plain sailing for Tung, a man reared in the traditions of a secretive and patriarchal Shanghainese family business empire where the chairman's every word was sacrosanct and his orders were carried out without question.
"Until three months ago I was in business," he confided to a panel of cnntral bankers attending a high powered International Monetary Fund (IMF) conference in Hong Kong earlier this month.
"For those of you who are in business, let me give you a piece of advice. Don't ever do what I'm doing now."

Life for Tung, who was born in the Chinese year of the ox and will be 60 in May, is now an endless round of lunch and dinner speaking engagements, of back-to-back high powered meetings to form a new administration, of pressing the flesh and -- new for him -- defending his views as he works to articulate his vision for a Hong Kong under China.
In the countdown to the handover at midnight on June 30, he has angered Hong Kong's energetic pro-democracy lobby by supporting China's plans to dilute civil liberties.

He has alientated Martin Lee, the leader of the Democracy Party, Hong Kong's largest. He accused Lee of "badmouthing" Hong Kong in his overseas speaking tours when he warns that its cherished freedoms are threatened.

He has complained that overseas governments, including the outgoing British and their allies in Europe and the United States don't understand. The post-handover changes to human rights laws are merely technical and pose no material changes, Tung says.
PROBLEMS WITH THE POLLS

Tung has already stumbled across some of the pitfalls of political life. Tycoons don't have to worry about opinion polls, but politicians do. "We are now masters of our own house," Tung said when he was appointed Hong Kong's Chief Executive-designate in December.
But a recent poll, conducted by the 1997 Transition Project at Hong Kong's Baptist University, drew a troubling conclusion for Hong Kong's first home-grown leader.
It found the burly, bristle-haired Tung, whose given names mean "Build China", was less popular with Hong Kong's 98 percent Chinese rank and file than the outgoing British governor.

Patten might be a light-haired, pale-eyed "foreign devil" who cannot speak Chinese and whose democratic reforms in the twilight of British rule sparked a vicious backlash of invective from an infuriated Beijing. But more than 60 percent of the 546 respondents said they were happy with Patten's performance.

Tung scored only 53 percent. Academic Michael DeGolyer put the disparity down to Tung's support for Chinese plans to roll back civil liberties after the handover and disrupt the status quo. "Hong Kong people are very satisfied with their lives and with their government," DeGolyer said.
FORGED IN THE TRADITIONS OF THE MOTHER OF PARLIAMENTS
Patten was born in 1944 -- the year of the monkey, according to the Chinese almanac.

When he took over in mid-1992, there were just five years to go before over a century and a half of British rule ended and the brash and wealthy coloy of six million people was handed over to Communist China.
Even by the testing standards of British parliamentary debates, Patten was regarded as possessing a silver tongue, a shrewd political brain and extensive administrative experience.

He served in the British government fom July 1989 to November 1990 as Secretary for State for Environment, one of the largest departments. Hong Kong civil servants say that stood him in good stead for running Hong Kong's 180-strong influential civil service. Policy secretaries say he knows how to delegate.
Patten has said he pulled Tung into his inner core of advisers, the Executive Council, to tap the views of someone with political beliefs from the other side of the spectrum.
Tung publicly espouses Asian values of filial piety, consensus and the good of the community over the individual.

Tung has told interviewers his heroes are Lee Kuan Yew, Singapore's no-nonsense elder statesman, Deng Xiaoping, China's ruthless late paramount leader and right wing British former Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher -- values shared in Beijing but not necessarily in the freewheeling Hong Kong of the late 1990s.

Patten dismisses Asian values. He called them "piffle" in a newspaper column written earlier this year in which he argued a region as diverse as Asia could hardly be expected to subscribe to a common value system which he argued boiled down to nothing more than an attempt to justify authoritarianism.
TO PATTEN, RIGHTS OF INDIVIDUAL PARAMOUNT
He regards the rights to the individual as paramount. An ardent Roman Catholic, he is a fierce advocate of a free press and rambunctious political debate.
Patten also handles the media with skill, journalists say.

Tung can be testy with reporters, who dog his every step, and has complained about the way the foreign media -- who are in Hong Kong in force in the countdown to the handover -- depict events in the last days of colonial rule.

Patten has his detractors -- particularly in the ranks of Hong Kong's pro-China political parties and the long-standing British colonial business elite who took umbrage at a newcomer rocking the boat with reforms.
But he also has some ardent fans. He charms grandmothers, and children rush to touch him when he appears on one of his frequent walkabouts on the streets of Hong Kong.

His stock soared when he stepped on to the sun-baked tarmac at Hong Kong's Kai Tak airport on July 9, 1992 dressed in an ordinary suit and not the ostrich feathers, sword and tropical whites of a traditional colonial governor.

He embarked on a meet-the-people blitz in town halls, radio talk shows and the crowded streets of Hong Kong to the delight of ordinary people grown familiar with the rather aloof and remote style of previous inhabitants of Government House.
Tung has yet to find that common touch.
HIS OWN MAN OR CHINA'S MAN?
The eyes of defiantly capitalist Hong Kong are now fixed firmly on Tung. How will he demonstrate that he is no puppet of China?
China, after all, bailed out the Tung family shipping company a decade earlier. Will he treat the people of Hong Kong as shareholders or employees?

Does his enthusiastic backing for China's plans to dissolve the elected legislature and roll back certain civil liberties laws portend a lurch towards a more authoritarian rule for the freewheeling community long used to a light government touch?
How will he cope with a civil service reared in adversarial British tradition of robust debate, staffed by a self-confident, well-travelled and well-educated colonial elite.
"Compromise is not a dirty word," said Tung after China s 400-member Selection Committee overwhelmingly handed him the mandate to step into Patten's shoes.
But it's a lonely road ahead as Tung, who did not fight his way up through the political ranks and has no allies forged along the way, struggles to assemble his governing team.
